text.p: In a cliff-hanger vote, Portugal's parliament has rejected a left-wing bid to liberalise abortion that would have virtually allowed it on demand in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

After six hours of often heated debate, parliament voted by just 112 to 111 on Thursday against a call by the Young Socialists that would have swept away all restrictions to abortion in the first three months. The Young Socialists are affiliated to the ruling Socialists.

A virtually identical proposal by the small Communist Party was rejected by a wider margin in balloting in which the Socialists and their main conservative opposition had allowed a free vote with no set party line.
But a third resolution extending the period in which abortions can be carried out in cases of a deformed foetus to 24 weeks from the previous 16 weeks was approved by a big majority.
There was a brief moment of confusion after the vote on the Young Socialists' motion which initially appeared to have ended in a tie with 111 votes in favour and 111 against.
But the final result was 112 against after one deputy, whose vote had initially been missed, was included.
"The motion has been rejected," announced parliamentary speaker Antonio Almeida Santos to cheers and jeers from rival supporters who had packed the public gallery.

Supporters of reform had argued that the existing abortion law, passed 13 years ago in this Roman Catholic country of 10 million, was excessively restrictive, leading to a high number of illegal abortions.
Portugal allows abortion with no time limit in cases where the mother's life is in danger and in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy where her health, physical or psychological, is at serious risk.

But critics say the latter is interpreted so restrictively that the number of legal abortions carried out in this country -- just 275 in 1995 -- is no more than a drop in the ocean compared with the number of illegal terminations.
Health officials say bungled illegal abortions are one of the main causes of maternal mortality in the country.
The campaign ahead of the vote had generated fierce controversy, with anti-abortion groups running advertisements on television and in the newspapers against any change.

An image used by the Catholic, anti-abortion Together for Life group of a supposedly 12-week-old foetus, with the caption "would you kill this child", turned out to be that of a foetus several weeks older.

But the anti-abortion camp could count on the backing of a number of leading political figures, including Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, a practising Catholic, who announced he personally opposed any change to the existing legislation.
Communist leader Carlos Carvalhas, blaming Guterres' statement for the parliamentary result, said his party would continue to press for reform.
